options.B: Much cheaper, because the address space and resources are shared

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Context switching between threads of one process is also faster.

questions.question: Concurrency differs from parallelism in that:

options.A: Concurrency needs at least four cores
options.B: Concurrency means several tasks make progress (possible even on one core by interleaving); parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on different cores
options.C: Parallelism is possible on a single core only
options.D: They mean exactly the same thing

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A single-core system can be concurrent but not parallel.

questions.question: Running the same operation on different subsets of data on different cores (e.g. summing halves of an array) is:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Task parallelism distributes different tasks (operations) across cores.

questions.question: By Amdahl's law, an application that is 25% serial runs on 2 cores. The maximum speed-up is about:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Speed-up ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S)/N) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.375) = 1.6.

questions.question: If 50% of a program is serial, the maximum speed-up with any number of cores is:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: As N → ∞, speed-up → 1/S = 1/0.5 = 2.

questions.question: Which is a programming challenge of multicore systems?

options.C: Dividing work into balanced tasks, splitting data, handling data dependencies, and testing and debugging

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Silberschatz lists identifying tasks, balance, data splitting, data dependency, testing and debugging.

questions.question: User-level threads are:

options.B: Managed by a thread library in user space, without kernel support
options.C: Managed directly by the OS kernel

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Kernel threads are supported and scheduled directly by the OS.

questions.question: In the many-to-one model, if one thread makes a blocking system call:

options.A: The entire process blocks, and threads cannot run in parallel on multicore systems
options.C: A new kernel thread is created

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). All user threads share one kernel thread.

questions.question: The one-to-one model, used by Linux and Windows:

options.B: Maps all user threads to one kernel thread
options.C: Allows only one thread per process
options.D: Maps each user thread to its own kernel thread – more concurrency, but creating a user thread needs a kernel thread

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It allows threads to run in parallel on multiple cores.

questions.question: The two-level model is a variation of the many-to-many model that also:

options.C: Allows a user thread to be bound to a particular kernel thread

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: It combines many-to-many multiplexing with one-to-one binding.

questions.question: Which model lets other threads keep running when one thread blocks AND lets threads run in parallel on several cores?
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Many-to-one fails on both counts.

questions.question: Running two hardware threads on one core, so the core can switch to the other thread during a memory stall, is called:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: The OS sees each hardware thread as a logical CPU.

questions.question: The data structure that holds a thread's state (ID, registers, stack pointer, state) is the:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: A process's PCB points to the TCBs of its threads.

questions.question: A busy web server creates a separate thread for each client request mainly to:

options.D: Serve many clients at once and stay responsive

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Thread pools are usually used instead of creating a thread per request.

questions.question:
Match the multithreading model with its mapping:
a. Many-to-one
b. One-to-one
c. Many-to-many
d. Two-level

1. Many user threads onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads
2. Each user thread onto its own kernel thread
3. Many-to-many plus binding a user thread to a kernel thread
4. All user threads onto a single kernel thread
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Model matching is very common in KEA and KSET papers.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Threads of the same process share code and data.
II. Threads of the same process share one stack.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the many-to-one model, threads cannot run in parallel on a multicore system.
Reason (R): Only one thread can access the kernel at a time, because all share a single kernel thread.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: That is the main limitation of the model.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Concurrency is impossible on a single-core system.
Reason (R): On a single core, the CPU switches among tasks so quickly that several tasks make progress.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: R describes concurrency on one core, so A is false.

questions.question: An advantage of user-level threads over kernel-level threads is that:

options.A: Switching between them needs no kernel-mode privileges, so it is fast
options.B: They always run in parallel on many cores
options.C: A blocking system call never blocks the process
options.D: The kernel schedules each of them separately

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Their main drawback is that one blocking call can block the whole process (in many-to-one).

questions.question: Kernel-level threads are:

options.C: Managed only by a user library
options.D: Created, scheduled and managed directly by the operating system

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Linux, Windows and macOS all support kernel threads.

questions.question: A word processor that checks spelling in one thread while the user types in another mainly shows the multithreading benefit of:
questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: The program stays interactive even while part of it is busy.

questions.question: On a multiprocessor, a single-threaded process can use:

options.A: Only one processor at a time

questions.subject: Thread Concepts, Multicore Programming and Multithreading Models
questions.explanation: Multithreading lets one process benefit from several cores (scalability).

sets.name: 2 · Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues

questions.question: The three main thread libraries in use today are:

options.C: POSIX Pthreads, Windows threads and Java threads

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Pthreads may be provided as a user-level or kernel-level library.

questions.question: POSIX Pthreads is:

options.B: A specification (IEEE 1003.1c) for thread behaviour, not an implementation

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Programs include <pthread.h>.

questions.question: In Pthreads, a new thread is created with:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). pthread_join() makes the caller wait for that thread to finish.

questions.question: A thread ends its own execution in Pthreads by calling:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Returning from the thread function also ends it.

questions.question: In the Windows API, threads are created with ____ and waited for with ____.
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: WaitForMultipleObjects() waits for several threads.

questions.question: In Java, a thread can be created by:

options.A: Extending the Thread class or implementing the Runnable interface

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The code to run goes in the run() method.

questions.question: In Java, a new thread actually begins executing when the program calls:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: start() creates the thread and the JVM then calls run() in it.

questions.question: Java's join() method makes the calling thread:

options.D: Wait until the target thread terminates

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: It is similar to pthread_join().

questions.question: Implicit threading means that:

options.A: Threads are created by hardware only
options.B: Compilers and run-time libraries, not the programmer, create and manage the threads
options.D: Each user writes their own scheduler

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Examples: thread pools, fork-join, OpenMP, Grand Central Dispatch, Intel TBB.

questions.question: A thread pool improves performance because:

options.B: It removes the need for a CPU
options.C: An existing idle thread serves a request faster than creating a new thread, and the number of threads is limited
options.D: It creates a new thread for every request

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Java offers thread pools through ExecutorService.

questions.question: OpenMP supports parallel programming in C, C++ and Fortran mainly through:

options.B: Compiler directives such as #pragma omp parallel

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: The run-time creates as many threads as there are cores.

questions.question: In the fork-join model:

options.A: A parent task forks child tasks that run in parallel and then joins (waits for and combines) their results

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Java's ForkJoinPool implements this model for recursive divide-and-conquer tasks.

questions.question: Grand Central Dispatch, which schedules blocks of work on dispatch queues, was developed by:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Serial queues run blocks in order; concurrent queues run them in parallel.

questions.question: If one thread of a multithreaded program calls fork(), and exec() is called immediately after, the better choice is:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). exec() replaces the whole process image, so duplicating every thread would be wasted work.

questions.question: In a multithreaded program, a signal may be delivered to:

options.A: The thread to which it applies, every thread, certain threads, or a thread designated to receive all signals

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Synchronous signals go to the thread that caused them.

questions.question: Terminating a thread before it has completed is called:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The thread to be cancelled is the target thread.

questions.question: In asynchronous cancellation:

options.A: The target thread checks periodically whether it should terminate
options.D: One thread immediately terminates the target thread

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). In deferred cancellation the target checks at safe cancellation points.

questions.question: The default cancellation type in Pthreads is:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: A thread can create a cancellation point by calling pthread_testcancel().

questions.question: Data that each thread keeps its own copy of, such as a per-thread transaction ID, is called:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: TLS values persist across function calls, unlike local variables.

questions.question: In many-to-many and two-level models, the intermediate data structure that appears to the user-thread library as a virtual processor is the:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). With scheduler activations, the kernel informs the library about events through upcalls.

questions.question: Linux creates both processes and threads with the system call:

options.D: clone(), whose flags decide how much the child shares with the parent

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Linux calls both 'tasks'.

questions.question: Windows keeps the data of each thread in the structures:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: TEB (thread environment block) lives in user space.

questions.question: The number of threads in a thread pool is usually chosen based on:

options.C: The number of CPUs, the amount of memory and the expected number of concurrent requests

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Some pools adjust their size dynamically.

questions.question: Two threads increment a shared counter without a lock. The result may be wrong because of:
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Shared data must be protected with a mutex or other synchronization.

questions.question:
Match the Pthreads function with its job:
a. pthread_create()
b. pthread_join()
c. pthread_exit()
d. pthread_cancel()

1. Terminates the calling thread
2. Waits for a thread to finish
3. Requests termination of a target thread
4. Creates a new thread
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). API matching is common in KEA papers.

questions.question:
Match the implicit-threading technique with its description:
a. Thread pool
b. OpenMP
c. Fork-join
d. Grand Central Dispatch

1. Threads created at start-up that wait for work
2. Compiler directives that mark parallel regions
3. Apple's dispatch queues
4. Parent forks subtasks and later joins their results
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Implicit-threading approaches.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Deferred cancellation lets a thread terminate at a safe point.
II. Asynchronous cancellation is always safe for shared data.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Asynchronous cancellation may leave resources or shared data in an inconsistent state.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Thread pools usually serve requests faster than creating a new thread for each request.
Reason (R): An existing thread is reused instead of being created and destroyed.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Creation and destruction costs are avoided.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Calling run() directly on a Java Thread object starts a new thread.
Reason (R): The start() method creates a new thread, which then calls run().

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: Calling run() directly runs it in the current thread, so A is false.

questions.question: Intel Threading Building Blocks (TBB) is:

options.A: A C++ template library for designing parallel applications

questions.subject: Thread Libraries, Implicit Threading and Threading Issues
questions.explanation: It is another example of implicit threading.

sets.name: 1 · Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF

questions.question: Which of the following is not a CPU scheduling algorithm?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Rollback is a recovery action, not a scheduling algorithm. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Computer Operator P2 · Q71

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of First Come First Served (FCFS) scheduling algorithm?

options.A: It leads to starvation of processes
options.B: It may cause high waiting time for processes
options.C: It is a preemptive scheduling algorithm
options.D: It requires knowledge of burst times.

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Short jobs may wait behind a long one (convoy effect), so average waiting time can be high. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Junior Console Operator P2 · Q35

questions.question:
Consider the following processes and their burst times
Process – Burst Time: P₁ – 5, P₂ – 8, P₃ – 3, P₄ – 6, P₅ – 7
If the CPU scheduling is performed using Shortest Job First (SJF) (non-preemptive), then what will be the correct sequence of processes executed?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Shortest burst first: 3, 5, 6, 7, 8. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Junior Console Operator P2 · Q36

questions.question:
In SRT process scheduling algorithm, the arrival & execution time of the four processes are as follows.
Arrival time – Execution time – Process: 0 – 20 – P₁; 15 – 25 – P₂; 30 – 10 – P₃; 45 – 15 – P₄
What will be the process 'P₂' total waiting time?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: P₁ runs 0–20; P₂ runs 20–30, is preempted by P₃ (30–40), resumes 40–50; P₄ runs 50–65. P₂ waits (20 − 15) + (40 − 30) = 15. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q14

questions.question:
Consider a single processor system with four processes A, B, C and D represented as given below, where for each process the first value is its arrival time and second value is its CPU burst time
A(0, 10), B(2, 6), C(4, 3) and D(6, 7)
Which of the following options gives the average waiting time when preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) and the Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (NP-SJF) CPU scheduling algorithms are applied to the process?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: SRTF: A 0–2, B 2–4, C 4–7, B 7–11, D 11–18, A 18–26 → waits 16, 3, 0, 5 → 6. NP-SJF: A 0–10, C 10–13, B 13–19, D 19–26 → waits 0, 11, 6, 13 → 7.5. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2025 CS&A · Q42

questions.question: Consider the following set of processes that arrive at time 0 with length of the CPU burst time given in milliseconds: P1 = 26, P2 = 4, P3 = 5. What is the average waiting time for the processes that arrive in the orders P1, P2, P3 and P2, P1, P3 under FCFS policy?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Order 1: waits 0, 26, 30 → 56/3 ≈ 18.67. Order 2: waits 0, 4, 30 → 34/3 ≈ 11.33. Option 2 is the closest (truncated) value. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KEA 2026 CS Paper-2 · Q43

questions.question: ____ is invoked when there is a need to perform process scheduling, that is when a process from the ready queue is to be selected for dispatching to the CPU.
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: The short-term (CPU) scheduler picks the next ready process for the CPU. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2023 CS&A · Q22

questions.question: Process execution alternates between periods of computation and waiting for I/O. This is called the:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: CPU-bound processes have a few long bursts; I/O-bound processes many short ones.

questions.question: In preemptive scheduling:

options.A: The CPU can be taken away from a running process, e.g. when a higher-priority process arrives or a time slice ends
options.B: A process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling switches only when the running process terminates or waits.

questions.question: A good CPU scheduling algorithm tries to:

options.C: Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise turnaround, waiting and response times

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The five classic scheduling criteria.

questions.question: Turnaround time of a process is:

options.A: Time of first response − arrival time

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time.

questions.question: A process arrives at time 2, has a CPU burst of 5 and completes at time 10. Its waiting time is:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Turnaround = 10 − 2 = 8; waiting = 8 − 5 = 3.

questions.question: Response time, important in interactive systems, is the time from submission of a request until:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: It is different from turnaround time.

questions.question: The number of processes that complete their execution per unit time is called:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Higher throughput means more work done.

questions.question: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3 with bursts 24, 3 and 3 ms. Under FCFS the average waiting time is:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Waits 0, 24, 27 → 51/3 = 17. If the order were P2, P3, P1 the average would be (0 + 3 + 6)/3 = 3.

questions.question: The 'convoy effect' – many short processes waiting behind one long CPU-bound process – is typical of:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It lowers CPU and device utilisation.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time.

questions.question: Processes P1–P4 arrive at time 0 with bursts 6, 8, 7 and 3. Under non-preemptive SJF the average waiting time is:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF

questions.question: The main practical difficulty with SJF is that:

options.A: The length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance and must be predicted

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Predicted with exponential averaging: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n).

questions.question: Using exponential averaging with α = 0.5, a previous prediction τ = 10 ms and an actual last burst t = 6 ms, the next predicted burst is:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF

questions.question: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) is:

options.A: Round Robin with a small quantum
options.D: The non-preemptive version of priority scheduling

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: A newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time preempts the running one.

questions.question: A drawback of SJF and SRTF is that:

options.A: They have very high context-switch overhead in all cases
options.C: They cannot be used in batch systems
options.D: Long processes may starve if short ones keep arriving

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Ageing can be used to prevent starvation.

questions.question: The simplest CPU scheduling algorithm to implement, using a FIFO queue, is:
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: New processes join the tail; the CPU goes to the head.

questions.question:
Match the scheduling measure with its definition:
a. Turnaround time
b. Waiting time
c. Response time
d. Throughput

1. Processes completed per unit time
2. Time until the first response
3. Total time spent in the ready queue
4. Completion time − arrival time
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Criteria matching is common.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. SJF minimises the average waiting time.
II. FCFS is a preemptive algorithm.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: FCFS is non-preemptive.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): FCFS scheduling may cause the convoy effect.
Reason (R): Short processes have to wait behind a long CPU-bound process.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: That is the definition of the convoy effect.

questions.question: A Gantt chart in CPU scheduling shows:

options.D: Which process runs on the CPU during each interval of time

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Numerical scheduling questions are solved by drawing one.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm can be either preemptive or non-preemptive?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Priority scheduling can also be either.

questions.question: In a non-preemptive scheduler, a context switch to another process happens only when the running process:

options.A: Terminates or switches to the waiting state
options.C: Is interrupted by a higher-priority arrival

questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Windows 3.x and early Mac OS used cooperative (non-preemptive) scheduling.

questions.question: Which criterion matters MOST for an interactive (time-sharing) user?
questions.subject: Scheduling Criteria, FCFS, SJF and SRTF
questions.explanation: Users want the system to react quickly.

sets.name: 2 · Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: There are 10 different processes running on a workstation. Idle processes are waiting for an input event in the input Queue. questions.question:
Which of the following statement/statements is/are true?

questions.explanation: All three are true. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q2

questions.question:
Match the following with respect to scheduling algorithm

options.A: a - i, b - iii, c - iv, d - ii
options.B: a - ii, b - i, c - iv, d - iii
options.C: a - iv, b - iii, c - i, d - ii
options.D: a - iv, b - ii, c - iii, d - i

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: FCFS – arrival order; SJF – shortest burst; RR – arrival order with a fixed quantum; Priority – by priority. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q13

questions.question:

questions.question:

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm is used in realtime systems to ensure that critical processes meet their deadlines?

questions.question:

options.A: a – ii, b – iii, c – i, d – iv

questions.question: In Silberschatz's convention for priority scheduling:

options.D: A smaller priority number means a higher priority

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Starvation of low-priority processes in priority scheduling is solved by:

options.D: Ageing – gradually increasing the priority of waiting processes

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Round Robin scheduling is designed especially for:
questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It is FCFS with preemption after each time quantum.

questions.question: In Round Robin, if the time quantum is made very large, the algorithm behaves like:

questions.explanation: Then most processes finish in one quantum without too many switches.

questions.question: In a multilevel queue scheduler:

options.B: The ready queue is split into separate queues (e.g. foreground interactive, background batch), and a process stays permanently in one queue

options.D: Processes can move between queues – CPU-hungry processes move down, long-waiting ones move up

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It is the most general – and most complex – scheduling scheme.

questions.question: Rate-monotonic scheduling for periodic real-time tasks:

options.C: Assigns static priorities – the shorter the period, the higher the priority

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Processor affinity means:

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Windows schedules threads using a priority scheme with:
questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Lottery scheduling gives each process tickets and picks a random ticket. It is an example of:
questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: Kernel threads compete with all threads in the system (SCS).

questions.question:

questions.question:

options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: The quantum should be large compared with the context-switch time.

questions.question: In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) scheduling:

options.A: Each processor is self-scheduling, from a common or private ready queue

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: Which statement about preemptive priority scheduling is TRUE?

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling

questions.question: In Round Robin with n processes in the ready queue and quantum q, no process waits more than:

options.A: (n − 1) × q time units before its next quantum

questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: This bounded wait is why RR gives good response times.

questions.question: Which algorithm is most suitable for a batch system where all job lengths are known in advance and average waiting time must be minimal?
questions.subject: Priority, Round Robin, Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-time Scheduling
questions.explanation: SJF is optimal for average waiting time.

questions.question: A process needs to release all resources before it makes any requests for another resources. Select the true statement from the following.

questions.question: A deadlock is a situation in which:

options.A: A process is waiting for I/O to complete

questions.question: The four necessary conditions for deadlock (Coffman conditions) are:

options.A: Mutual exclusion, starvation, ageing and paging
options.B: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait
options.C: Hold and wait, preemption, spooling and swapping
options.D: Circular wait, thrashing, paging and segmentation

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the necessary conditions for deadlock?

questions.question: In a resource-allocation graph, an edge Pi → Rj means:

options.C: Resource Rj is assigned to Pi

questions.question: If every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph:

options.D: Implies that a deadlock has occurred

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention

options.B: Prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery, or ignoring the problem

questions.question: Deadlock prevention works by:

options.A: Granting requests only in safe states

questions.explanation: Avoidance uses extra information to stay in safe states.

questions.question: The mutual-exclusion condition generally cannot be denied for:

questions.explanation: Spooling a printer is one way around it.

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention

questions.explanation: Its resources are implicitly preempted.

questions.question: Three processes each need at most 2 units of a resource. The minimum number of units that guarantees no deadlock is:

questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). n(k − 1) + 1 = 3 × 1 + 1 = 4.

questions.question: Four processes each need at most 3 tape drives. The minimum number of drives that guarantees freedom from deadlock is:

questions.question: In a livelock:

options.D: Processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention
questions.explanation: Unlike deadlocked processes, livelocked processes are not blocked.

options.A: Is always part of a cycle

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention
questions.explanation: In deadlock, none of the processes in the set can proceed.

questions.explanation: Only the printer daemon uses the printer directly.

questions.question:

1. A resource can be used by only one process at a time

questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention

questions.question:

Which is/are correct?

questions.explanation: No cycle means no deadlock.

questions.question: Ignoring deadlocks and rebooting when one occurs is jokingly called the:
questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention
questions.explanation: It is used when deadlocks are rare and prevention is costly.

questions.question: A classic deadlock example: P1 holds the scanner and waits for the printer, while P2 holds the printer and waits for the scanner. Which condition is clearly visible?
questions.subject: Deadlock Conditions, Resource-allocation Graph and Prevention

questions.question: Deadlock is possible only if the system has at least:

options.C: It detects deadlocks after they occur
