options.B: Wait-for graph – a cycle means deadlock

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It is obtained from the resource-allocation graph by removing the resource nodes.

questions.question: For resources with several instances, the deadlock-detection algorithm:

options.A: Is similar to the Banker's safety algorithm, using Available, Allocation and Request matrices

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Processes that cannot finish are deadlocked.

questions.question: How often the detection algorithm should run depends mainly on:

options.B: How often deadlocks are likely to occur and how many processes they affect

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: It can run on every request, periodically, or when CPU utilisation drops.

questions.question: The two basic approaches to recovering from deadlock are:
questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Termination: abort all deadlocked processes or one at a time until the cycle disappears.

questions.question: When choosing a victim for abortion or preemption, the system considers:

options.A: Priority, how long the process has computed, resources used and needed, and how many processes must be aborted
options.B: Only the alphabetical order of names
options.C: Only the size of the program file

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: The aim is minimum cost.

questions.question: If the same process is always picked as the victim during resource preemption, the result is:

options.C: Starvation – fixed by including the number of rollbacks in the cost

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Rollback returns the victim to a safe earlier state.

questions.question: The Banker's algorithm gets its name because a bank:

options.A: Keeps resources in a vault forever
options.B: Lends only to the oldest customer
options.D: Never lends cash in a way that leaves it unable to satisfy all its customers' maximum needs

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Dijkstra framed the problem as a banker and customers.

questions.question:
Match the strategy with its approach:
a. Deadlock prevention
b. Deadlock avoidance
c. Deadlock detection
d. Deadlock recovery

1. Abort or preempt to break an existing deadlock
2. Grant a request only if the state stays safe
3. Periodically look for cycles in the wait-for graph
4. Ensure one of the four conditions can never hold
questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Strategy matching is a favourite question.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every unsafe state is a deadlock.
II. In a safe state, the OS can avoid deadlock by allocating carefully.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: An unsafe state may lead to deadlock but is not one yet.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Banker's algorithm needs each process's maximum claim in advance.
Reason (R): It must check that every process can still finish (a safe sequence) before granting a request.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Without maximum claims, the safety check is impossible.

questions.question: In the Banker's safety algorithm, when a process Pi can finish, the vector Work is updated as:
questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Pi releases everything it holds.

questions.question: Which of these is a deadlock PREVENTION technique rather than a recovery technique?

options.A: Preempting a resource from a victim
options.C: Requiring every process to request all resources at the start

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: It denies the hold-and-wait condition.

questions.question: Which method requires the most advance information about processes?
questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Avoidance needs each process's maximum demands.

questions.question: Aborting all deadlocked processes at once is:

options.D: Certain to break the deadlock, but expensive because their work is lost

questions.subject: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), Detection and Recovery
questions.explanation: Aborting one at a time is cheaper but needs repeated detection.

sets.name: 1 · Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation

questions.question:
Match List-I (Address binding & space) with List-II (Performed by):
(a) Compile time
(b) Load time
(c) Logical address
(d) Physical address
(i) One loaded into the memory address register
(ii) Generated by CPU
(iii) Relocatable code must be generated by compiler
(iv) Absolute code can be generated

options.A: a – iv, b – iii, c – ii, d – i
options.B: a – iii, b – iv, c – i, d – ii
options.C: a – iv, b – i, c – ii, d – iii
options.D: a – iii, b – ii, c – i, d – iv

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Silberschatz: compile-time binding gives absolute code, load-time binding needs relocatable code, the CPU generates logical addresses, and the MAR holds physical ones. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KEA 2026 CS Paper-2 · Q51

questions.question: ____ helps to control memory wastage occurring in dynamic partitioning.
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Compaction shuffles memory contents to merge scattered free holes (external fragmentation) into one block. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2023 CS&A · Q25

questions.question:
Which of the following memory management techniques can cause fragmentation?
a. Paging
b. Segmentation
c. Contiguous Allocation
d. Virtual Memory
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: The key counts external fragmentation: variable-sized pieces (segments, contiguous partitions) leave scattered holes. Paging only wastes part of the last page (internal fragmentation). (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Junior Console Operator P2 · Q45

questions.question: The best fit and first fit strategies for memory allocation suffer from
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Both carve variable-sized holes out of free memory, so the free space gets broken into small scattered pieces. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: PGCET 2024 M.Tech CS · Q25

questions.question:
Match the following with respect to various memory management:
a. Demand paging
b. Segmentation
c. Dynamic partitions
d. Fixed partitions
(i) Degree of multiprogramming
(ii) Working set
(iii) Supports user view of memory
(iv) Compaction

options.A: a – ii, b – iv, c – iii, d – i
options.B: a – ii, b – iii, c – i, d – iv
options.C: a – iv, b – iii, c – ii, d – i
options.D: a – ii, b – iii, c – iv, d – i

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Demand paging uses working sets; segmentation matches the user's view; dynamic partitions need compaction; fixed partitions fix the degree of multiprogramming. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2025 CS&A · Q45

questions.question: If addresses are bound at execution time, what is needed?

options.A: Hardware support – a memory-management unit (MMU) with a relocation register
options.B: Absolute code generated by the compiler
options.C: The process must always be loaded at the same location

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Execution-time binding lets a process move in memory during execution; most general-purpose OSs use it.

questions.question: In which address-binding scheme do the logical and physical addresses differ?
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Compile-time and load-time binding produce identical logical and physical addresses; execution-time binding gives different (virtual) addresses.

questions.question: The relocation register contains 14000. A user process generates logical address 346. The physical address is:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The MMU adds the relocation (base) value to every logical address: 14000 + 346.

questions.question: A process has base register 300040 and limit register 120900. Which is the last legal physical address of the process?
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Legal addresses run from base to base + limit − 1 = 300040 + 120900 − 1.

questions.question: In contiguous allocation, memory protection is provided by:

options.C: Relocation (base) and limit registers, checked on every address

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: An address greater than or equal to the limit causes a trap (addressing error) to the operating system.

questions.question: A routine is not loaded until it is called; all routines are kept on disk in relocatable format. This is:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Dynamic loading gives better memory use because an unused routine (e.g. error handling) is never loaded.

questions.question: With dynamic linking, a small piece of code that tells how to locate the library routine is called a:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Shared libraries (DLLs) are linked at execution time through stubs.

questions.question: Moving a process temporarily out of main memory to a backing store and later bringing it back for continued execution is called:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A swap variant used with priority scheduling is called roll out, roll in.

questions.question: The major part of swap time is:

options.A: Transfer time, proportional to the amount of memory swapped
options.D: Time to build the page table

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: That is why swapping a small process is quicker; mobile OSs avoid swapping altogether.

questions.question: A 100 MB process is swapped to a disk with a transfer rate of 50 MB per second (ignore latency). What is the total time to swap it out and to swap in another 100 MB process?
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 100 / 50 = 2 s each way, so 2 + 2 = 4 s.

questions.question: Fixed (static) partitioning of memory mainly suffers from:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: A small process in a large fixed partition wastes the rest of that partition; the number of partitions also limits multiprogramming.

questions.question: Variable (dynamic) partitioning, where each process gets exactly the memory it needs, mainly suffers from:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: As processes leave, memory is broken into many small scattered holes.

questions.question: The allocation strategy that searches the list of holes and allocates the first hole that is big enough is:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: First fit is generally the fastest; next fit starts searching from where the last search ended.

questions.question: Which allocation strategy allocates the smallest hole that is big enough and so leaves the smallest leftover hole?
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Best fit must search the whole list unless it is kept ordered by size.

questions.question: Worst-fit allocation gives a process:

options.D: A hole of a power-of-two size

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: The idea is that the leftover hole will be large enough to be useful.

questions.question: Memory holes of 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB (in order) receive processes of 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB and 426 KB (in order). Which strategy places all four processes?
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Best fit: 212→300, 417→500, 112→200, 426→600. First fit and worst fit leave 426 KB waiting.

questions.question: With the holes 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB, 600 KB and first-fit allocation of 212 KB and then 417 KB, the 417 KB process goes into the:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: 212 KB takes the 500 KB hole (288 KB left); the first hole that can hold 417 KB is the 600 KB one.

questions.question: Statistical analysis of first fit shows that for N allocated blocks about 0.5 N blocks are lost to fragmentation. This is known as the:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: It means up to one-third of memory may be unusable.

questions.question: Compaction is possible only if:

options.A: Relocation is dynamic and done at execution time
options.D: Binding is done at compile time

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Moving a process needs its addresses to be rebound, which only execution-time binding allows.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Internal fragmentation is unused memory inside an allocated partition.
II. External fragmentation means enough total free memory exists but it is not contiguous.
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Both definitions are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Paging suffers from no external fragmentation.
Reason (R): Any free frame can be allocated to a process that needs it.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Paging can still have internal fragmentation in the last frame of a process.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Compaction removes internal fragmentation.
Reason (R): Compaction moves memory contents to place all free memory together in one block.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Compaction attacks external fragmentation; internal fragmentation stays inside the allocated blocks.

questions.question: In a buddy system with a 256 KB segment, a request for 21 KB is given a block of:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Blocks are split into halves until the smallest power of two ≥ 21 KB (32 KB) is reached; 11 KB is internal fragmentation.

questions.question: A technique that keeps in memory only the instructions and data needed at a given time, so that a program larger than memory can run, is:
questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: Overlays were designed by the programmer and need no special OS support.

questions.question: Two solutions to external fragmentation are:

options.A: Increasing the time quantum and priority aging
options.B: Larger fixed partitions and best fit

questions.subject: Address Binding, Contiguous Allocation, Swapping and Fragmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Non-contiguous allocation lets a process use whatever free memory is available.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?

options.A: To map virtual memory addresses to physical addresses
options.C: To cache the results of arithmetic operations
options.D: To store data for frequently accessed programs

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The TLB is a small, fast associative cache of recent page-table entries (page → frame). (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Junior Console Operator P2 · Q100

questions.question: The purpose of TLB (Translational Lookaside Buffer) is :
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Without a TLB every reference needs two memory accesses (page table + data). (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: PGCET 2023 M.Tech CS · Q30

questions.question:
In a system using paging with Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), what will be the Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT), if the memory access time is 100 ns, TLB access time is 20 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 80%?
Assume TLB hit requires one memory access and TLB miss requires two.
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: 0.8 × (20 + 100) + 0.2 × (20 + 200) = 96 + 44 = 140 ns. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2025 CS&A · Q44

questions.question:
Paging is a memory management scheme that permits
(a) The physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous
(b) Physical memory is divided into fixed sized blocks called pages
(c) Eliminates the need for compaction
(d) Logical memory is divided into blocks of the same size called frames
Which of the aforementioned statements are correct?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Physical blocks are frames and logical blocks are pages, so (b) and (d) swap the names; paging has no external fragmentation, so no compaction. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KEA 2026 CS Paper-2 · Q45

questions.question: If the page size is 2048 bytes and a process needs 72766 bytes, find the total number of frames allocated and what is the internal fragmentation?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: 72766 / 2048 = 35.53 → 36 frames = 73728 bytes; 73728 − 72766 = 962 bytes wasted. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KEA 2026 CS Paper-2 · Q48

questions.question: In paging, physical memory is divided into fixed-sized blocks called ____ and logical memory into blocks of the same size called ____.
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Page size equals frame size; it is a power of 2 (typically 4 KB).

questions.question: A logical address in paging is divided into:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The page number indexes the page table; the offset is added to the frame's base address.

questions.question: A logical address space of 2^m bytes uses pages of 2^n bytes. The page number is given by:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The low-order n bits are the page offset.

questions.question: A system has 32-bit logical addresses and a 4 KB page size. How many entries can a single-level page table have?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 4 KB = 2^12, so 32 − 12 = 20 bits form the page number.

questions.question: Page size 1 KB; page 2 of a process is held in frame 5. The logical address 2100 maps to physical address:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 2100 = 2 × 1024 + 52, so page 2, offset 52 → 5 × 1024 + 52 = 5172.

questions.question: With 16-bit logical addresses and a page size of 1 KB, the number of pages in the logical address space is:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation

questions.question: Paging still suffers from:

options.A: Internal fragmentation (on average half a page per process)

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The last page of a process is rarely full.

questions.question: The page table of each process is located through which register?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Changing page tables on a context switch only needs the PTBR to be reloaded; the page-table length register (PTLR) gives its size.

questions.question: Without a TLB, a paged memory reference needs how many memory accesses?

options.C: Two – one for the page-table entry and one for the data

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). This doubles the access time, which the TLB removes on a hit.

questions.question: The TLB hit ratio is 90%, memory access takes 100 ns and TLB search time is negligible. What is the effective access time?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation

questions.question: Address-space identifiers (ASIDs) in TLB entries are used to:

options.D: Identify each process, so the TLB need not be flushed on every context switch

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Without ASIDs the TLB must be flushed when another process runs.

questions.question: A valid–invalid bit attached to each page-table entry indicates:

options.B: Whether the page has been modified
options.D: Whether the page is in the process's logical address space

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). An access to an invalid page traps to the OS; protection bits mark read-only or read–write pages.

questions.question: Paging makes it easy to share code among processes. Such shareable code must be:

options.B: Reentrant (pure) code that never changes during execution

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Example: one copy of a text editor or the standard C library mapped into many processes.

questions.question: Which page-table structure keeps one entry per physical frame rather than one per page?
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: It saves memory but makes lookup slower; it was used on the IBM PowerPC and UltraSPARC.

questions.question: Large 32/64-bit address spaces avoid huge single page tables by using:

options.D: Hierarchical paging, hashed page tables or inverted page tables

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Two-level paging pages the page table itself (outer page table + inner page table).

questions.question: A memory-management scheme that supports the programmer's view of memory as a collection of variable-sized units such as main program, functions, stack and arrays is:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A logical address is a pair <segment-number, offset>.

questions.question: Each entry of a segment table contains:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The STBR points to the segment table and the STLR gives the number of segments.

questions.question: Segment 2 has base 4300 and limit 400. The logical address <2, 53> maps to:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 53 < 400, so physical = 4300 + 53 = 4353.

questions.question: Segment 0 has base 1400 and limit 1000. What happens for the logical address <0, 1222>?

options.C: Trap – addressing error, because 1222 exceeds the limit

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: The offset must be less than the limit; otherwise the hardware traps to the OS.

questions.question: Segmentation suffers from:
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Segments are of different sizes, so variable-sized holes appear – like dynamic partitioning.

questions.question: Segmented paging (segmentation with paging) is used to:

options.B: Remove external fragmentation of segments by paging each segment

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Intel IA-32 combines segmentation and paging.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Paging is visible to the programmer, segmentation is not.
II. In paging the page size is decided by the hardware.
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Paging is invisible to the programmer; segmentation reflects the program's logical structure.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A TLB greatly reduces the effective memory-access time of paging.
Reason (R): Programs show locality of reference, so most translations are found in the TLB.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: Hit ratios above 99% are common on modern processors.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In pure paging the logical address space of a process must be contiguous in physical memory.
Reason (R): A page table maps each page to any free frame.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: A is false – paging lets the physical address space be non-contiguous; R is true.

questions.question:
Match the following:
a. Paging
b. Segmentation
c. TLB
d. Inverted page table
1. Fixed-size blocks
2. Variable-size logical units
3. Cache of page-table entries
4. One entry per frame
questions.subject: Paging, TLB and Segmentation
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Matching the memory-management terms is common in KEA / KSET papers.

sets.name: 1 · Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing

questions.question: Consider a computer system that supports 32-bit physical as well as virtual addresses. Now since the space of the physical address is same as the virtual address, the operating system designers would decide to entirely get rid of its virtual memory. Which one of the following is true in this case?

options.A: It is no longer possible to efficiently implement multi-user support.
options.B: It is possible to make CPU scheduling more efficient now.
options.C: There would no longer be required for hardware support for memory management.
options.D: It would be possible to make the processor cache organization more efficient now.

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Without virtual memory there are no virtual-to-physical translations, so the MMU / page-table hardware is not needed (GATE 2016 question). (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q6

questions.question: The lowest number of page frames that are bound to be allocated in an environment of virtual memory to a running processes is determined by

options.C: the size of the physical memory
options.D: the total number of processes in memory

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: The minimum is set by the most memory references a single instruction can make (operands, indirection), i.e. by the ISA. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q18

questions.question: The performance of process in virtual memory depends on the rate at which its components have to be loaded into memory to achieve a low rate of loading of process components virtual memory manager uses the
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Programs reference a small set of pages at a time (locality of reference), so keeping that set in memory keeps page faults low. (Official answer: KEA final key, GTTC recruitment 2024.)
questions.source: GTTC 2024 Lecturer CS · Q53

questions.question: Mapping of file is managed by
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: The official key gives the file system, which keeps track of where each file's blocks are (its metadata maps the file to disk blocks). (Official answer: KEA final key, GTTC recruitment 2024.)
questions.source: GTTC 2024 Technician Gr-III CS (C1) · Q29

questions.question: Which of the following is not correct about the virtual memory management?

options.A: It is not necessary to load all of the segments of a process
options.C: It has large virtual address space
options.D: It provides lower degree of multiprogramming

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Virtual memory raises the degree of multiprogramming, since only part of each process need be in memory. (Option 2 holds for segmented virtual memory, which the question refers to.) (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2025 CS&A · Q46

questions.question: Virtual memory is a technique that:

options.B: Allows the execution of processes that are not completely in main memory
options.C: Removes the need for main memory
options.D: Increases the size of the CPU cache

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Programs can be larger than physical memory, and more programs can run at the same time.

questions.question: In demand paging, a page is brought into memory:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: A pager that never brings in a page until it is needed is a 'lazy swapper'.

questions.question: When a process refers to a page that is not in main memory, the hardware raises a:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The valid–invalid bit of the page-table entry is 'invalid'.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps of handling a page fault in order:
1. Find a free frame
2. Trap to the OS and check that the reference is valid
3. Read the page from disk into the frame
4. Update the page table and restart the instruction
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: If no frame is free, a page-replacement algorithm chooses a victim.

questions.question: Starting a process with no pages in memory and bringing in each page only on its first fault is called:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Prepaging brings in several pages at once to avoid the initial burst of faults.

questions.question: Memory access time is 200 ns, the average page-fault service time is 8 ms and the page-fault rate is p. The effective access time is:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). EAT = (1 − p) × memory access + p × page-fault time; even p = 1/1000 makes EAT about 8.2 µs.

questions.question: Memory access takes 100 ns, servicing a page fault takes 10 ms, and the page-fault rate is 1 in 100,000 accesses. The effective access time is about:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing

questions.question: Copy-on-write lets a parent and child process created by fork():

options.C: Share pages until one of them writes, when a copy of that page is made

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: vfork() goes further – the parent is suspended and the child uses its address space.

questions.question: The 'modify' or 'dirty' bit of a page tells the OS that:

options.B: The page has been changed and must be written to disk before replacement
options.D: The page belongs to the kernel

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). An unmodified page can simply be overwritten, halving the page-fault service time.

questions.question: Thrashing is a situation in which:

options.A: A process spends more time paging than executing
options.C: The CPU is fully used by useful work

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). CPU utilisation falls sharply as the degree of multiprogramming rises too far.

questions.question: The main cause of thrashing is:

options.A: Processes not having enough frames to hold their working set

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: When the total demand (sum of working-set sizes) exceeds available frames, thrashing starts.

questions.question: The set of pages referenced in the most recent Δ page references is called the:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Denning's working-set model; Δ is the working-set window.

questions.question: A strategy to prevent thrashing by setting upper and lower bounds on each process's page-fault rate is the:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Too many faults → give the process more frames; too few → take frames away.

questions.question: Equal allocation of 93 frames among 5 processes gives each process:

options.B: 18 frames, with 3 left as a free-frame buffer

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: 93 / 5 = 18 remainder 3.

questions.question: Under proportional allocation with 62 free frames, processes of 10 pages and 127 pages get about:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 10/137 × 62 ≈ 4 and 127/137 × 62 ≈ 57.

questions.question: With global replacement, a process selects a replacement frame:

options.A: From the set of all frames, even one belonging to another process

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Local replacement chooses only from the process's own frames; global replacement gives better throughput.

questions.question: Mapping a disk file into part of a process's virtual address space, so that file I/O becomes ordinary memory access, is called:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: On Linux it is done with mmap(); several processes can map the same file to share memory.

questions.question: Allocating memory to the kernel from physically contiguous pages, in power-of-two blocks, uses the:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: The slab allocator is the other kernel scheme, using caches of objects.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Demand paging may increase the degree of multiprogramming.
II. In demand paging, a page that is never referenced is never loaded.
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Both are advantages of demand paging.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Increasing the degree of multiprogramming always increases CPU utilisation.
II. Thrashing can be reduced by suspending some processes.
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Beyond a point utilisation drops (thrashing); swapping out processes frees frames for the rest.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Programs can run efficiently under demand paging even though only part of them is in memory.
Reason (R): Programs show locality of reference.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Locality keeps the page-fault rate low.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Thrashing raises CPU utilisation.
Reason (R): During thrashing, processes keep waiting for the paging device.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Utilisation falls during thrashing because processes are queued for paging I/O.

questions.question: Locking a page in memory so that it cannot be replaced is done with a:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: Useful for pages that are the target of an I/O transfer in progress.

questions.question: The area of a disk used to hold pages that are not in main memory is called:
questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Windows uses a page file; Linux a swap partition or swap file.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of virtual memory?

options.A: A program can be larger than physical memory
options.B: It always makes every memory access faster
options.C: Less I/O is needed to load or swap programs

questions.subject: Demand Paging, Page Faults, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
questions.explanation: A page fault makes that access far slower; the gains come from better memory use.

sets.name: 2 · Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations

questions.question:
Consider that a virtual memory system uses a FIFO page replacement policy. For a process, it allocates a fixed number of frames. Now consider the following statements.
A: An increase in the number of page frames that are allocated to a process sometimes leads to an increase in page fault rate.
B: A few programs do not display the locality of reference.
Which one of the following option is correct?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: A is Belady's anomaly, possible with FIFO; B is also true – some programs (e.g. jumping through large data) show poor locality. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q8

questions.question:
Which of the following page replacement algorithms can lead to optimal performance?
a. Least Recently Used (LRU)
b. Optimal Page Replacement
c. FIFO
d. Second Chance
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: The key takes Optimal (the true minimum) and LRU, its best practical approximation; FIFO and second chance can be far from optimal. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Junior Console Operator P2 · Q51

questions.question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the page replacement algorithms and its principle.

options.A: NRU (Not Recently Used) - Removes a page at random from the lowest numbered nonempty class
options.C: LRU -Throw out the page that has been used for the longest time
options.D: Second chance - Simple modification of FIFO

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: LRU throws out the page that has NOT been used for the longest time. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: PGCET 2023 M.Tech CS · Q70

questions.question: Applying FIFO page replacement for the reference string →7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3. The main memory can accommodate 3 pages. How many page faults will occur?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Faults on 7, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3 – only the first re-use of 0 is a hit. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: PGCET 2026 CS · Q55

questions.question:
Match the following:
i. Kernel
ii. Belady's anomaly
iii. Paging
iv. Free-space management
(a) Ensures efficient storage utilization
(b) Avoids external fragmentation
(c) Provides basic low-level operations
(d) Increase in the number of page frames leads to increase in the number of page faults

options.A: i – d, ii – c, iii – b, iv – a
options.B: i – b, ii – d, iii – a, iv – c
options.C: i – c, ii – d, iii – b, iv – a
options.D: i – b, ii – a, iii – d, iv – c

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Kernel = low-level services; Belady = more frames, more faults (FIFO); paging avoids external fragmentation; free-space management uses storage well. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KSET 2025 CS&A · Q47

questions.question: The page-replacement algorithm that replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It gives the lowest possible fault rate but needs future knowledge, so it is used as a benchmark.

questions.question: Belady's anomaly can occur with which page-replacement algorithm?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never show the anomaly.

questions.question: For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with FIFO replacement, the number of page faults with 3 frames and with 4 frames is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The classic example of Belady's anomaly – more frames, more faults.

questions.question: Reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames. The number of page faults under FIFO is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Silberschatz's standard string: FIFO 15, LRU 12, Optimal 9.

questions.question: For the same reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames, LRU gives:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). LRU = 12 lies between Optimal (9) and FIFO (15).

questions.question: For the reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames, the optimal algorithm gives:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: No algorithm can do better with 3 frames.

questions.question: With 3 frames, initially empty, and LRU replacement, how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Faults on 1, 2, 3, 4 (replaces 2), 5 (replaces 3); the second reference to 1 is a hit.

questions.question: With 3 frames, initially empty, and FIFO replacement, how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 4 replaces 1, then 1 replaces 2, then 2 replaces 3 – every reference faults.

questions.question: Which hardware support is commonly used to approximate LRU?

options.C: A reference bit for each page

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: The bit is set when the page is referenced; the OS clears and checks it periodically.

questions.question: The second-chance (clock) algorithm is a modification of:

options.B: FIFO, giving a page with its reference bit set another chance

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: The pointer moves around a circular list, clearing reference bits until it finds a page with bit 0.

questions.question: In the enhanced second-chance algorithm, the best page to replace has (reference bit, modify bit) =
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). (0, 0) – neither recently used nor modified, so it needs no write-back.

questions.question: The algorithm that replaces the page with the smallest reference count is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: MFU replaces the page with the largest count, arguing that a small count means it was just brought in.

questions.question: LRU can be implemented exactly using:

options.A: A counter (time-of-use) per page or a stack of page numbers

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: With a stack, the most recently used page is on top and the LRU page at the bottom.

questions.question: Page buffering algorithms keep:

options.A: A pool of free frames, so a faulting page can be read in before the victim is written out

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: This reduces the time a process waits on a page fault.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. LRU is a stack algorithm.
II. FIFO never suffers from Belady's anomaly.
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: FIFO can suffer from the anomaly; LRU and Optimal cannot.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The optimal algorithm needs knowledge of future references.
II. The optimal algorithm is used mainly to compare other algorithms.
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Both are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): LRU does not suffer from Belady's anomaly.
Reason (R): The set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1 frames.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: That 'inclusion property' defines stack algorithms.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): FIFO replaces the page that has been used least recently.
Reason (R): FIFO replaces the oldest page in memory.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: FIFO replaces the oldest loaded page, even if it is used heavily – that is LRU's idea, not FIFO's.

questions.question: A page reference string of length 20 contains 6 distinct pages. With any page-replacement algorithm and frames initially empty, the minimum number of page faults is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Each distinct page must be loaded at least once (compulsory faults).

questions.question: For n distinct pages in a reference string of length p, the maximum number of page faults is:
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: At worst every reference is a fault.

questions.question: Which statement about increasing the number of frames given to a process is generally true for LRU?

options.B: The number of page faults always increases
options.C: It has no effect on faults
options.D: The number of page faults never increases

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: LRU is a stack algorithm, so more frames never hurt.

questions.question: With 4 frames and Optimal replacement, how many page faults occur for 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: Faults: 1, 2, 3, 4 (compulsory), 5 (replaces 4, used last), and 4 again near the end = 6. FIFO with 4 frames gives 10.

questions.question:
Match the algorithm with its idea:
a. FIFO
b. LRU
c. Optimal
d. LFU

1. Page that will not be used for the longest time
2. Oldest page in memory
3. Page with the smallest use count
4. Page not used for the longest time
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A frequent KEA / KSET matching question.

questions.question: In page-replacement terms, a 'victim' page is:

options.A: A page with a hardware error
options.C: The page chosen to be removed from memory to make room
options.D: The first page of a program

questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: If the victim's dirty bit is set it is written to disk first.

questions.question: Which algorithm is easiest to implement but often performs poorly?
questions.subject: Page Replacement – FIFO, Optimal, LRU and Approximations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It needs only a queue of the pages in memory.
